clue.text: Straighten out - but it's exhausting! (10)

indicators.note: Out here means out of true: a thing knocked out no longer sits the way it was set, so the letters in front of it lose their order.

blocks.note: ten letters, and exactly the ten wanted once they are dealt out again

explanation.walkthrough: The dash invites you to read two definitions, tidying and tiring. There is only one: the instruction to straighten is itself the thing put out of order.
explanation.definitionFit: exhausting → SHATTERING: British usage takes it well past merely tiring, to a weariness that feels like being broken apart.

clue.text: Heard prophet sizzle (4)

indicators.note: What is heard arrives as sound alone, so the clue is describing how a word is pronounced and leaving the spelling to you.

blocks.note: a seer is one who sees what is to come, which is a prophet's trade, and aloud it can be written the other way

explanation.walkthrough: Three words and four letters, so nothing is being assembled. 'Heard prophet' reads as a sentence, which hides that the first word is an instruction rather than part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: sizzle → SEAR: to sear meat is to scorch its surface in a hot pan, and the noise that makes is the definition, verb for verb.

clue.text: Slowly, learner's lost mighty ship (4)

indicators.note: What is lost is gone from where it stood, so the letter named just before drops out of the word it was sitting in.

blocks.note: largo is the musical direction to play at a slow, broad tempo
L is the plate a British driving learner has to display on the car

explanation.walkthrough: The comma dresses the first word as an adverb attached to the sentence, when it is the whole of the fodder. Both conventions here are standing ones: the tempo marking and the L-plate.
explanation.definitionFit: mighty ship → ARGO: definition by example, the great galley Jason sailed after the Golden Fleece with fifty heroes aboard.

clue.text: Race brother pathetically - he's seen in the lead (11)

indicators.note: To do a thing pathetically is to do it badly, and a word handled badly comes out with its letters in the wrong places.

blocks.note: eleven letters from a sprint and a sibling, to be dealt out again

explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' looks like a definition and 'in the lead' like a finishing position, so the athletics stays in your head throughout. Both belong to the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: he's seen in the lead → TORCHBEARER: the runner carrying the Olympic flame heads the procession, so being out in front is the whole of the job.

clue.text: Made another recording of French father that's stuck up (7)

indicators.note: A notice stuck up climbs the wall it is fixed to, and in a down entry climbing means reading the assembled letters from the bottom.

blocks.note: de is the French word for of
pater is Latin for father and survives in British public-school slang as a name for one's dad

explanation.walkthrough: 'French father' pulls you straight to PERE, and that is the trap. Split the words the other way — 'of French', then 'father' on its own — and two pieces appear.
explanation.definitionFit: Made another recording → RETAPED: the RE- prefix means doing it over, and taping was how a recording got made before discs and files.

clue.text: Songs in book (7)

blocks.note: a number is one item on a programme — a single song or dance performed as one turn
the fourth book of the Old Testament, titled for the two censuses of the Israelites it records

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and the middle one only joins the other two. Nothing is spelled out here, which is why so short a clue can hold so long an answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Songs → NUMBERS: a number is a single turn on a bill; and 'book' → NUMBERS, the Old Testament book whose title is itself a plural.

clue.text: Still, India's supposed mountain-dweller (4)

blocks.note: both words mean up to now, as in 'is he here still?'
I is India in the NATO spelling alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes the first word look like a discourse marker opening a sentence about the subcontinent. It is the first chunk, and the country is only a radio-alphabet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: supposed mountain-dweller → YETI: the ape-like creature said to walk the high Himalaya, with 'supposed' admitting nobody has produced one.

clue.text: Air battle across the Continent? (10)

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: fighters and dogfights over occupied Europe, war in the sky
the reading the setter meant: an air is an old word for a tune, and the fight is between countries each sending one song

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing comes apart into letters here; the question mark is the tell. Once 'air' stops being sky and starts being melody, the whole clue settles into one annual televised contest.
explanation.definitionFit: Air battle across the Continent? → EUROVISION: read straight, the clue describes Europe's yearly televised competition of songs, one entry per country.

clue.text: Cross Italian footballers given Belgium: maybe buck up (10)

indicators.note: Maybe admits the word beside it is only one instance of what is wanted, so you climb from the male animal to the name of its kind.
In a down entry up runs towards the top of the grid, so the four letters just found are written out starting from the bottom.

blocks.note: Internazionale of Milan, known everywhere by the first half of its name
B is Belgium's international vehicle registration letter
a buck is the male of the species, so the general word for the animal is what is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a transfer story and the colon is punctuation for it, nothing more. 'Cross' is the definition and means to mate one strain with another, not to be annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross → INTERBREED: a breeder who crosses two strains puts them together to produce young, the stockman's verb rather than the bad-tempered adjective.

clue.text: Procedures for solving problems as clattering hailstorm overwhelms golf (10)

indicators.note: A clatter is the noise of loose things falling about, and letters falling about are not going to land where they started.
To overwhelm is to engulf, so the single letter that follows is swallowed into the mix rather than left standing beside it.

blocks.note: nine letters of weather, waiting to be dealt out again
G is golf in the NATO spelling alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clattering hailstorm' is one picture, which makes it easy to read both words as scenery. Only the noun is fodder; the participle in front of it is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Procedures for solving problems → ALGORITHMS: step-by-step recipes a computer or a person follows to reach a result, one settled method per task.

clue.text: Determination regularly exhibited by Geraint (4)

indicators.note: Doing a thing regularly means doing it at a fixed interval, and the interval here is one: take a letter, skip a letter, all the way through.

blocks.note: the first letter of the name and then every other one after it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly exhibited by' sounds like a phrase about character, which is what makes it easy to read past as padding. Geraint is a Welsh name, here only a supply of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Determination → GRIT: the crossword's favourite sense of the word, courage that keeps going under pressure, borrowed from the hard sand that gives a wheel purchase.

clue.text: Axed before 50, Everyman's at end of career, an irrelevance (7,5)

indicators.note: What comes before goes in front, so the first chunk is placed ahead of the Roman numeral rather than after it.
The end of a word is its final letter, and that one letter is all this takes from the word it points at.

blocks.note: to axe something is to chop it, and the past tense carries across
fifty in Roman numerals
the setter talking about himself: Everyman's here is I've, short for I have
the last letter of this word

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs every puzzle, so his name in a clue is the setter saying 'I'. The definition is the aside tacked on at the end, and the comma is the only warning of the switch.
explanation.definitionFit: an irrelevance → CHOPPED LIVER: from the complaint 'What am I, chopped liver?', so the phrase names something treated as of no account.

clue.text: Statesman: Gee! Old Glory aflutter! (5,6)

indicators.note: A flag aflutter is flapping loose in the wind, and letters flapping loose will not stay in the order they were handed to you.

blocks.note: an exclamation plus the flag's nickname, eleven letters between them

explanation.walkthrough: Old Glory is the nickname of the flag of the United States, so 'aflutter' reads as bunting on a pole. The colon after 'Statesman' is doing the same job a dash would.
explanation.definitionFit: Statesman → LLOYD GEORGE: definition by example — the Liberal prime minister who led Britain through the last years of the First World War.

clue.text: Sportsperson damaged golf-club (4-6)

blocks.note: a knee or an engine described as shot is wrecked past use
the club used on the green, the one that rolls the ball at the hole

explanation.walkthrough: Three words and a story about a broken golf club, which is exactly the wrong sport. The hyphen in the clue also sits in a different place from the hyphen in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sportsperson → SHOT-PUTTER: definition by example, the athlete whose event is heaving a heavy metal ball as far as possible from the shoulder.

clue.text: Servants in the auditorium: but how many in the audience? (10)

indicators.note: An auditorium is a room built for listening, so the word before it is to be judged by ear rather than by its spelling.

blocks.note: attendants are the servants who wait on someone, and spoken aloud that plural is indistinguishable from the word wanted

explanation.walkthrough: The colon and the question mark make this look like two separate thoughts about a theatre. The middle phrase belongs to the first half, as an instruction to listen.
explanation.definitionFit: how many in the audience → ATTENDANCE: the count of people present at an event, the figure a theatre or a stadium announces afterwards.

clue.text: Madman seen in Psycho (the adaptation) (7)

indicators.note: If a thing can be seen in something else it is already there, so the letters are sitting untouched inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: seven letters in a row starting in the middle of the film title and running on past the bracket

explanation.walkthrough: The italics and the brackets dress this as a note about which version of the film is meant, and that is the disguise: punctuation never interrupts a hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: Madman → HOTHEAD: a loose fit rather than a clinical one — someone whose temper goes off without warning, reckless rather than actually ill.

clue.text: North, then south, track circling: back! (7)

indicators.note: To circle a thing is to go all the way round it, so the word beside the instruction closes about the letters already named.

blocks.note: a spoor is the trail of prints and scent an animal leaves for a hunter to follow
the two compass initials, taken in the order the clue sets them out

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark makes the last word read as a shout at a dog on a trail. It is the definition, and it means to fund something rather than to retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: back → SPONSOR: to back a venture is to put money behind it, the financial sense of the verb rather than the physical one.

clue.text: Some loathe - or embrace - idea (7)

indicators.note: Some asks for a part and not the whole, so only a stretch of the letters in front of you is wanted.

blocks.note: seven letters in a row, beginning inside the first word and finishing inside the last

explanation.walkthrough: 'Embrace' is doing everything it can to look like an instruction to put one thing inside another. It is fodder, and the two dashes are there to break the run up.
explanation.definitionFit: idea → THEOREM: a proposition proved from axioms, so 'idea' is the loose everyday cover a setter puts over a precise mathematical noun.

clue.text: At sea, ark teems with small flying kind of a mammal (7)

indicators.note: To be at sea is to be adrift with no bearings, so the letters beside it are in no settled order.
Something flying has taken off and gone, so the letter named just before it leaves the mix before anything is rearranged.

blocks.note: S is the size printed on a clothing label for small
eight letters, less the one named just before, leaving seven to deal out again

explanation.walkthrough: 'With small flying' reads as insects over the water, which is the picture the surface wants. It is an instruction: one letter goes before any shuffling happens.
explanation.definitionFit: kind of a mammal → MEERKAT: definition by example — the small southern African mongoose that stands upright on its hind legs to watch for danger.

clue.text: I'm grateful to get support embracing prince who'll become a frog (7)

indicators.note: An embrace closes round whatever is held, so the word before it opens up and takes the letter named after it inside.

blocks.note: ta is the everyday British word for thanks
the dole is British unemployment benefit, state support for those out of work
P is the standard abbreviation for prince

explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' wants to be a pole or a prop, and it is the benefit money instead. In the fairy tale of the surface a frog turns into a prince, which is the wrong way round here.
explanation.definitionFit: who'll become a frog → TADPOLE: the larval stage, all tail and gills, that grows legs and turns into the adult amphibian.

clue.text: Unusual issue characteristic of Pitt the Elder? (7)

blocks.note: issue in its old legal sense of a person's offspring, and three arriving at once is well out of the ordinary
stop reading the name as an eighteenth-century prime minister and count the letter T as the two words run together

explanation.walkthrough: Pitt the Elder was a British prime minister, and the clue is banking on you searching his family history. Write the words out instead: PiTT THe puts three Ts in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Unusual issue → TRIPLET: issue is the formal word for offspring, and three born at once is the unusual case; the run of Ts is the second sense.

clue.text: Rashly endure drivel; fail to make good on promise (12)

definitions.text: fail to make good on promise

indicators.note: To act rashly is to act with no care for order or consequence, so what stands beside it comes out in no particular arrangement.

blocks.note: twelve letters between the two words, which is the whole supply needed

explanation.walkthrough: The semicolon is the join: wordplay to the left of it, definition to the right. 'Rashly endure' reads as one act of impatience, and that is what hides the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: fail to make good on promise → UNDERDELIVER: office jargon for producing less than you said you would, measured against the boast that came first.

clue.text: Present the northern fruit that's offered up (4)

indicators.note: What is offered up is raised towards whoever takes it, and in a down entry raised means the letters are read from the bottom of the grid.

blocks.note: in northern English speech 'the' is clipped to a single t', as in down t'pit
one of the shortest fruits in the language, which is why setters reach for it so often

explanation.walkthrough: 'Present the northern fruit' reads as one instruction to hand something over, so the definition looks like it runs on. It stops after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Present → GIFT: a plain synonym, two nouns for a thing handed over for nothing, though only one of them also means a natural talent.

clue.text: Exhausting grandeur of showbusiness primarily displayed here? (4)

definitions.text: Exhausting grandeur of showbusiness primarily displayed here?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so each word in the run ahead of it surrenders its opening letter and nothing more.

blocks.note: the opening letters of these four words, read straight off in the order they stand

explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: the same four words spell the answer out of their initials and describe it at the same time, with 'displayed here' pointing back at the clue itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue says self-importance is what the entertainment industry chiefly puts on show, and that is what the word names.

clue.text: Ultimately prudent to learn mingling; one would lose grip without partner at the barbecue (4)

definitions.text: one would lose grip without partner at the barbecue

indicators.note: The ultimate letter of a word is its very last one, and that final letter is taken from each word in the run that follows.

blocks.note: the last letter of this word
the last letter, which in a two-letter word is half of it
the last letter of this word
the last letter, from the word planted here to look like a shuffling instruction

explanation.walkthrough: The semicolon marks the switch to the definition, which is long and jokey enough to look like the whole clue. Tongs come in pairs, so a single one drops the sausage.
explanation.definitionFit: one would lose grip without partner at the barbecue → TONG: the singular of tongs, a pair of arms that only pinch when both are present.

clue.text: Broadcaster backing poet (German) gallivanting (10)

indicators.note: Backing here means lending support rather than turning anything round, and it does no more than set the broadcaster against the piece beside it — loose, as joins go.

blocks.note: Sky is the British satellite television company
Philip Larkin, the Hull librarian who became one of Britain's best-known post-war poets
G is the dictionary abbreviation for German

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a broadcaster funding a German poet, a sentence plausible enough to stop you looking any further. The definition is the single word at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: gallivanting → SKYLARKING: both mean larking about to no serious purpose, one leaning towards roaming for pleasure and the other towards high-spirited mischief.

clue.text: It may be a Fisherman's Dance (4)

blocks.note: 'may be' flags an example: the thing meant belongs to an angler, who winds his line back onto it
a brisk Scottish and Irish country dance in which the couples wheel round one another

explanation.walkthrough: The capital letters make the clue look like the title of a piece of music, which is the whole of the misdirection. Both halves are ordinary senses of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: It may be a Fisherman's → REEL: the spool an angler winds his line onto; and 'Dance' → REEL, the whirling Scottish and Irish country dance.

clue.text: Laws covering alien little figures (10)

indicators.note: To cover a thing is to lie over it and hide it, so the word in front goes right round the letters named next.

blocks.note: statutes are laws as written down and passed by a parliament
the extraterrestrial of the film, and the crossword's standard alien

explanation.walkthrough: 'Laws covering alien' reads as immigration policy, which is exactly the sentence the setter wants in your head. The definition is the two words at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: little figures → STATUETTES: small sculpted models of a person or an animal, the mantelpiece size rather than the public-square size.
